Spotted barracudina (Arctozenus risso) is a mesopelagic fish of the family Paralepididae that attains a maximum recorded total length of 29 centimeters [Li = 29 centimeters]. Field surveys conducted in the North Atlantic indicate that individuals typically achieve this asymptotic size after several years of growth in cold, deep waters. Like many paralepidids, this species exhibits an elongated, slender body form well-suited to an active predatory lifestyle in the midwater environment. Reproductive maturation in Arctozenus risso occurs at a comparatively smaller body size, with the onset of gonad development recorded at a total length of 14.7 centimeters [Lp = 14.7 centimeters]. This pubertal length threshold marks the transition from juvenile foraging to the allocation of energy toward gamete production, a shift that coincides with a measurable increase in body mass. The wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 10.4 grams [Wwp = 10.4 grams], derived from length–weight relationships established for specimens collected across its geographic range. These morphometric benchmarks are essential for parameterizing population dynamics models and for assessing the species' vulnerability to pelagic fisheries bycatch.

Regarding the earliest life stages, the age at birth—defined as the time from egg extrusion to hatching—has been documented as 83 days [ab = 83 days] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. This protracted incubation period is characteristic of cold-water, high-latitude teleosts and reflects the temperature-dependent kinetics of embryonic development. The wet weight at birth of the larvae, measured immediately after eclosion, is 0.0038 grams [Wwb = 0.0038 grams]. This minute mass corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 1.9 millimeters, a value commonly reported for paralepidids that produce relatively small, pelagic eggs. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first weeks of exogenous feeding commencement, a critical window in which mortality rates are typically high. Following hatching, the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase, during which it must successfully transition to active prey capture before the energy stores are fully exhausted.

Reproductive output in Arctozenus risso is low relative to many other mesopelagic teleosts, consistent with the species' slow life-history pace in cold, low-productivity waters. Under a thermal regime of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], the maximum reproductive rate corresponds to approximately 3.6 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3.6 eggs per day], a value inferred from the product of clutch size and spawning frequency. Gravid females produce approximately 370 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 370 eggs per spawning event], with an estimate of roughly 3.6 such events occurring annually [F_R_i = roughly 3.6 such events occurring annually] based on examinations of ovarian histology. This relatively low fecundity is balanced by the extended lifespan of the species, which allows for multiple reproductive seasons over an individual's lifetime. The reproductive strategy of iteroparous, batch-spawning adults is typical of deep-dwelling fishes that experience stable, cold thermal environments year-round.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been estimated at 87.5 grams [Wwi = 87.5 grams], a value that corresponds to a total length of 29 centimeters [Li = 29 centimeters] through the allometric growth equation typical for this family. This adult body mass represents a substantial investment in somatic growth, particularly given the low metabolic rates associated with life at temperatures near 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. The maximum lifespan of Arctozenus risso in the wild is approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years], a figure derived from otolith increment analysis of specimens collected during research trawls in the Labrador Sea and a at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]djacent waters. This longevity is comparable to that of other midwater predators such as lanternfishes and bristlemouths, which also exhibit slow growth and delayed maturation in cold, food-limited environments. The age-specific mortality schedule appears to be relatively low during the adult stage, with senescence becoming apparent only after the completion of multiple spawning seasons.

The timing of sexual maturation relative to birth has been determined through examination of gonadal development in field-caught individuals. The time since birth at puberty, defined as the interval from hatching to the first histological evidence of vitellogenic oocytes in females or spermatogenesis in males, is approximately 6 years since birth [tp = approximately 6 years since birth] under natural thermal conditions of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. This remarkably long juvenile phase, exceeding half the total lifespan, reflects a life-history strategy in which delayed reproduction is traded off against increased somatic growth and reduced adult mortality. The pubertal wet weight of 10.4 grams [Wwp = 10.4 grams] is reached concurrently with the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, initiating a reproductive career that may span another five years. Such a delayed onset of reproduction is thought to buffer population fluctuations in the variable deep-sea environment, ensuring that only well-conditioned individuals contribute to the next generation. These demographic parameters are crucial for informing conservation assessments of this species, which is increasingly encountered as incidental bycatch in deep-water fisheries.
